# cosmic_text/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0
[2](https://docs.rs#2)
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! # COSMIC Text
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! This library provides advanced text handling in a generic way. It provides abstractions for
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! shaping, font discovery, font fallback, layout, rasterization, and editing. Shaping utilizes
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! harfrust, font discovery utilizes fontdb, and the rasterization is optional and utilizes
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! swash. The other features are developed internal to this library.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! It is recommended that you start by creating a [`FontSystem`], after which you can create a
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! [`Buffer`], provide it with some text, and then inspect the layout it produces. At this
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! point, you can use the `SwashCache` to rasterize glyphs into either images or pixels.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! ```
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! use cosmic_text::{Attrs, Color, FontSystem, SwashCache, Buffer, Metrics, Shaping};
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! // A FontSystem provides access to detected system fonts, create one per application
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! let mut font_system = FontSystem::new();
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! // A SwashCache stores rasterized glyphs, create one per application
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! let mut swash_cache = SwashCache::new();
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! // Text metrics indicate the font size and line height of a buffer
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! let metrics = Metrics::new(14.0, 20.0);
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! // A Buffer provides shaping and layout for a UTF-8 string, create one per text widget
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! let mut buffer = Buffer::new(&mut font_system, metrics);
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! // Borrow buffer together with the font system for more convenient method calls
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! let mut buffer = buffer.borrow_with(&mut font_system);
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! // Attributes indicate what font to choose
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! let attrs = Attrs::new();
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! // Set size and text
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! buffer.set_size(Some(80.0), Some(25.0));
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! buffer.set_text("Hello, Rust! 🦀\n", &attrs, Shaping::Advanced, None);
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! // Inspect the output runs
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! for run in buffer.layout_runs() {
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     for glyph in run.glyphs.iter() {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!         println!("{:#?}", glyph);
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!     }
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! }
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! // Create a default text color
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! let text_color = Color::rgb(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF);
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! // Draw the buffer (for performance, instead use SwashCache directly)
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! buffer.draw(&mut swash_cache, text_color, |x, y, w, h, color| {
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!     // Fill in your code here for drawing rectangles
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! });
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! ```
[54](https://docs.rs#54)
[55](https://docs.rs#55)// Not interested in these lints
[56](https://docs.rs#56)#![allow(clippy::new_without_default)]
[57](https://docs.rs#57)// TODO: address occurrences and then deny

# FontSystem in cosmic_text - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cosmic-text/latest/cosmic_text/struct.FontSystem.html

`pub struct FontSystem { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Access to the system fonts.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-FontSystem)

### impl [FontSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.FontSystem.html)

Create a new [ FontSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.FontSystem.html), that allows access to any installed system fonts

[§](https://docs.rs#timing)Timing

This function takes some time to run. On the release build, it can take up to a second,
while debug builds can take up to ten times longer. For this reason, it should only be
called once, and the resulting [ FontSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.FontSystem.html) should be shared.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/font/system.rs.html#213-273)#### pub fn [new_with_locale_and_db_and_fallback](https://docs.rs#method.new_with_locale_and_db_and_fallback)(

) -> Self

Shape lines until scroll, resolving any pending dirty state first.

This processes dirty flags (invalidating caches for lines that need reshaping or relayout) and then shapes/layouts visible lines.

Call this before reading layout results via [ layout_runs](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html#method.layout_runs) or

[when working with the](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html#method.hit)

`hit``Buffer` directly. The [wrapper calls this automatically.](https://docs.rs/struct.BorrowedWithFontSystem.html)

    &attrs,
    Shaping::Advanced,
    None,

# skrifa - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/skrifa/0.40.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/skrifa/index.html

## Expand description

A robust, ergonomic, high performance crate for OpenType fonts.

Skrifa is a mid level library that provides access to various types
of [ metadata](https://docs.rs/trait.MetadataProvider.html) contained in a font as well as support
for loading glyph

[.](https://docs.rs/outline/index.html)

`outlines`It is described as “mid level” because the library is designed to sit
above low level font parsing (provided by [ read-fonts](https://crates.io/crates/read-fonts))
and below a higher level text layout engine.

See the [readme](https://github.com/googlefonts/fontations/blob/main/skrifa/README.md)
for additional details.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub extern crate`- [read_fonts](https://docs.rs/read-fonts/0.37.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/read_fonts/index.html)as raw;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Primary attributes typically used for font classification and selection.
- [bitmap](https://docs.rs/bitmap/index.html)
- Bitmap strikes and glyphs.
- [charmap](https://docs.rs/charmap/index.html)
- Mapping of characters (codepoints, not graphemes) to nominal glyph identifiers.
- [color](https://docs.rs/color/index.html)
- Drawing color glyphs.
- [font](https://docs.rs/font/index.html)
- Basic representation of an in-memory font resource.
- [instance](https://docs.rs/instance/index.html)
- Helpers for selecting a font size and location in variation space.
- [metrics](https://docs.rs/metrics/index.html)
- Global font and glyph specific metrics.
- [outline](https://docs.rs/outline/index.html)
- Loading, scaling and hinting of glyph outlines.

- Useful collection of common types suitable for glob importing.

- Definitions for specifying variations and typographic features.

# fontdb - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fontdb/0.23.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/fontdb/index.html

## Expand description

`fontdb` is a simple, in-memory font database with CSS-like queries.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- The database can load fonts from files, directories and raw data (`Vec<u8>`).
- The database can match a font using CSS-like queries. See `Database::query`.
- The database can try to load system fonts. Currently, this is implemented by scanning predefined directories. The library does not interact with the system API.
- Provides a unique ID for each font face.

[§](https://docs.rs#non-goals)Non-goals

-
Advanced font properties querying.
 The database provides only storage and matching capabilities. For font properties querying you can use[ttf-parser](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/ttf-parser).
-
A font fallback mechanism.
 This library can be used to implement a font fallback mechanism, but it doesn’t implement one.
-
Application’s global database.
 The database doesn’t use`static`, therefore it’s up to the caller where it should be stored.
-
Font types support other than TrueType.

[§](https://docs.rs#font-vs-face)Font vs Face

A font is a collection of font faces. Therefore, a font face is a subset of a font. A simple font (*.ttf/*.otf) usually contains a single font face, but a font collection (*.ttc) can contain multiple font faces.

`fontdb` stores and matches font faces, not fonts.
Therefore, after loading a font collection with 5 faces (for example), the database will be populated
with 5 `FaceInfo` objects, all of which will be pointing to the same file or binary data.

[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

The database performance is largely limited by the storage itself.
We are using [ttf-parser](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/ttf-parser), so the parsing should not be a bottleneck.

On my machine with Samsung SSD 860 and Gentoo Linux, it takes ~20ms to load 1906 font faces (most of them are from Google Noto collection) with a hot disk cache and ~860ms with a cold one.

On Mac Mini M1 it takes just 9ms to load 898 fonts.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

The library relies on memory-mapped files, which is inherently unsafe. But since we do not keep the files open it should be perfectly safe.

If you would like to use a persistent memory mapping of the font files,
then you can use the unsafe [ Database::make_shared_face_data](https://docs.rs/struct.Database.html#method.make_shared_face_data) function.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Database](https://docs.rs/struct.Database.html)
- A font database.
- [Face](https://docs.rs/struct.FaceInfo.html)- Info
- A single font face info.
- [ID](https://docs.rs/struct.ID.html)
- A unique per database face ID.
- [Query](https://docs.rs/struct.Query.html)
- A database query.
- [Weight](https://docs.rs/struct.Weight.html)
- Specifies the weight of glyphs in the font, their degree of blackness or stroke thickness.

`iter_order_by`)1.5.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/iter/traits/iterator.rs.html#3810-3814)[§](https://docs.rs#method.partial_cmp)#### fn [partial_cmp](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.partial_cmp)<I>(self, other: I) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/iter/traits/iterator.rs.html#3810-3814)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.partial_cmp)

#### fn [partial_cmp](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html#method.partial_cmp)<I>(self, other: I) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)>

[Lexicographically](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html#lexicographical-comparison)compares the

[elements of this](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)

`PartialOrd`[with those of another. The comparison works like short-circuit evaluation, returning a result without comparing the remaining elements. As soon as an order can be determined, the evaluation stops and a result is returned.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)

Compares and returns the minimum of two values.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/buffer.rs.html#66-113)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/buffer.rs.html#66-113)

Return an iterator of `(x_left, x_width)` pixel spans for the highlighted areas
between `cursor_start` and `cursor_end` within this run.

For pure LTR or pure RTL runs this yields at most one span. For mixed BiDi runs (where selected and unselected glyphs interleave visually) it yields multiple disjoint spans.

Returns an empty iterator if the cursor range does not intersect this run.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/buffer.rs.html#120-142)#### pub fn [cursor_position](https://docs.rs#method.cursor_position)(&self, cursor: &[Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/buffer.rs.html#120-142)

#### pub fn [cursor_position](https://docs.rs#method.cursor_position)(&self, cursor: &[Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)>

Returns the visual x position (in pixels) of `cursor` within this run,
or `None` if the cursor does not belong to this run.

For RTL glyphs the cursor is placed at the right edge minus the offset; for LTR glyphs it is placed at the left edge plus the offset.

Find which glyph in this run contains `cursor`, returning
`(glyph_index, pixel_offset_within_glyph)`, or `None` if the cursor
is not on this run.

# LineEnding in cosmic_text - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cosmic-text/latest/cosmic_text/enum.LineEnding.html

```
pub enum LineEnding {
    Lf,
    CrLf,
    Cr,
    LfCr,
    None,
}
```
## Expand description

Line ending

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Lf)

### Lf

Use `\n` for line ending (POSIX-style)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CrLf)

### CrLf

Use `\r\n` for line ending (Windows-style)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Cr)

### Cr

Use `\r` for line ending (many legacy systems)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LfCr)

### LfCr

Use `\n\r` for line ending (some legacy systems)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.None)

### None

No line ending

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/edit/vi.rs.html#269-272)#### pub fn [save_point](https://docs.rs#method.save_point)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/edit/vi.rs.html#269-272)

#### pub fn [save_point](https://docs.rs#method.save_point)(&mut self)

Set current change as the save (or pivot) point.

A pivot point is the last saved index. Anything before or after the pivot indicates that the editor has been changed or is unsaved.

Undoing changes down to the pivot point sets the editor as unchanged. Redoing changes up to the pivot point sets the editor as unchanged.

Undoing or redoing changes beyond the pivot point sets the editor to changed.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/edit/vi.rs.html#275-280)#### pub fn [set_passthrough](https://docs.rs#method.set_passthrough)(&mut self, passthrough: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Takes the buffered value if in state `Self::Unused`.

Path command.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.MoveTo)

### MoveTo([Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html))

Begins a new subpath at the specified point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LineTo)

### LineTo([Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html))

A straight line from the previous point to the specified point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CurveTo)

A cubic bezier curve from the previous point to the final point with two intermediate control points.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.QuadTo)

A quadratic curve from the previous point to the final point with one intermediate control point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Close)

### Close

Closes a subpath, connecting the final point to the initial point.

# Shaping in cosmic_text - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cosmic-text/latest/cosmic_text/enum.Shaping.html

```
pub enum Shaping {
    Basic,
    Advanced,
}
```
## Expand description

The shaping strategy of some text.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Basic)

### Basic

Basic shaping with no font fallback.

This shaping strategy is very cheap, but it will not display complex scripts properly nor try to find missing glyphs in your system fonts.

You should use this strategy when you have complete control of the text and the font you are displaying in your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Advanced)

### Advanced

Advanced text shaping and font fallback.

You will need to enable this strategy if the text contains a complex script, the font used needs it, and/or multiple fonts in your system may be needed to display all of the glyphs.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# lellm_derive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lellm-derive/0.4.6/lellm_derive/

## Expand description

lellm-derive — 派生宏与属性宏。

[§](https://docs.rs#%E4%B8%89%E7%BA%A7-api)三级 API

[§](https://docs.rs#level-1-tool-%E5%87%BD%E6%95%B0%E5%AE%8F%E6%8E%A8%E8%8D%9095-%E7%94%A8%E6%88%B7)Level 1: `#[tool]` 函数宏（推荐，95% 用户）

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use lellm_agent::ToolResult;
use lellm_derive::tool;
#[tool(name = "search", description = "搜索互联网信息")]
async fn search(query: String, limit: Option<u32>) -> ToolResult {
    // 实现逻辑
    Ok(format!("搜索结果: {}", query))
}
// 无依赖 — 直接调用生成的工厂函数：
builder.tool(search_tool());
// 有依赖 — 使用 _with 后缀工厂函数：
let client = SearchClient::new();
builder.tool(search_tool_with({
    let client = client.clone();
    move |args| async move {
        client.search(&args.query, args.limit).await
    }
}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#level-2-derivetool-struct-%E5%AE%8F%E9%AB%98%E7%BA%A7%E7%94%A8%E6%88%B7)Level 2: `#[derive(Tool)]` struct 宏（高级用户）

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use lellm_agent::ToolResult;
use lellm_derive::Tool;
#[derive(Tool, JsonSchema)]
#[tool(name = "search", description = "搜索互联网信息")]
struct SearchArgs {
    /// 搜索关键词
    query: String,
    /// 返回数量
    limit: Option<u32>,
}
// 注册：
let reg = SearchArgs::safe(|args| async move {
    Ok(format!("搜索结果: {}", args.query))
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#level-3-toolregistrationsafe%E6%A1%86%E6%9E%B6%E5%BC%80%E5%8F%91%E8%80%85)Level 3: `ToolRegistration::safe()`（框架开发者）

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use lellm_agent::{ToolDefinition, ToolRegistration};
let reg = ToolRegistration::safe(
    ToolDefinition {
        name: "search".to_string(),
        description: "搜索".to_string(),
        parameters: serde_json::json!({
            "type": "object",
            "properties": { "query": { "type": "string" } }
        }),
    },
    |args| async { Ok(args["query"].as_str().unwrap().to_string()) }
);
```

# lellm_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lellm-core/0.4.6/lellm_core/

## Expand description

lellm-core — 协议对象，零运行时依赖。

定义 LLM 交互的核心数据结构：Message, ContentBlock, ChatRequest, ChatResponse, ToolCall, ToolDefinition, TokenUsage, LlmError 等。

本 crate 是纯粹的协议层（Protocol Crate），类似 openai-types / anthropic-types 的统一抽象。Provider、Agent、Graph 都依赖于此，但它不依赖任何运行时。

# mermaid_rs_renderer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mermaid-rs-renderer/0.3.0/mermaid_rs_renderer/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#mmdr---fast-mermaid-diagram-renderer)mmdr - Fast Mermaid Diagram Renderer

A pure Rust implementation of Mermaid diagram rendering, providing 100-600x faster rendering than mermaid-cli by eliminating browser dependencies.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use mermaid_rs_renderer::{render, render_with_options, RenderOptions};
let diagram = r#"
flowchart LR
    A[Start] --> B{Decision}
    B -->|Yes| C[OK]
    B -->|No| D[Cancel]
"#;
// Simple one-liner
let svg = render(diagram).unwrap();
// With options
let svg = render_with_options(diagram, RenderOptions::default()).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline-control)Pipeline Control

For more control over the rendering pipeline, use the individual stages:

```
use mermaid_rs_renderer::{parse_mermaid, compute_layout, render_svg};
use mermaid_rs_renderer::{Theme, LayoutConfig};
let diagram = "flowchart LR; A-->B-->C";
// Stage 1: Parse
let parsed = parse_mermaid(diagram).unwrap();
// Stage 2: Layout
let theme = Theme::modern();
let config = LayoutConfig::default();
let layout = compute_layout(&parsed.graph, &theme, &config);
// Stage 3: Render
let svg = render_svg(&layout, &theme, &config);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-diagram-types)Supported Diagram Types

- **Flowcharts**(- `flowchart`/- `graph`): TD, TB, LR, RL, BT directions
- **Sequence Diagrams**(- `sequenceDiagram`)
- **Class Diagrams**(- `classDiagram`)
- **State Diagrams**(- `stateDiagram-v2`)
- **ER Diagrams**(- `erDiagram`)
- **Pie Charts**(- `pie`)
- **XY Charts**(- `xychart`)
- **Quadrant Charts**(- `quadrantChart`)
- **Gantt**(- `gantt`)
- **Timeline**(- `timeline`)
- **Journey**(- `journey`)
- **Mindmap**(- `mindmap`)
- **Git Graph**(- `gitGraph`)

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Pure Rust, no browser or Node.js required
- ~3ms cold start vs ~2500ms for mermaid-cli
- ~15MB memory vs ~300MB for mermaid-cli
- SVG and PNG output (PNG via resvg)
- Customizable themes and layout configuration

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

- `cli`
- `png`

For minimal dependencies (e.g., embedding in other tools like Zola):

```
[dependencies]
mermaid-rs-renderer = { version = "0.2.2", default-features = false }
```

# trifle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/trifle/0.5.0/trifle/

## Expand description

`trifle` — embedded, typo-tolerant trigram fuzzy search backed by SQLite.

trifle indexes short text segments and answers typo- and partial-tolerant queries, returning
matches that each carry where they matched. It owns a single SQLite store holding the segment
text, the caller key, and an inverted index (a base-plus-delta CRoaring posting per token),
and ranks by rarity-weighted shared-token overlap, counted bit-sliced in the
[ trifle_overlap](https://docs.rs/trifle-overlap/0.5.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/trifle_overlap/index.html) engine. The store is a derived, rebuildable cache over a caller-owned
source of truth; trifle never touches the caller’s data store.

It targets large corpora of small documents (≲ 1–2 KB per segment) read often and written infrequently. It is a fuzzy lexical overlap engine: rarer shared grams weigh more, and rarity is normalized per script class so a CJK bigram and a Latin trigram compare fairly. There is no BM25 or relevance tier.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use trifle::{Config, Index, Schema, SearchOpts};
let dir = tempfile::tempdir().unwrap();
let index = Index::open_at(&dir.path().join("trifle.db"), Schema::flat(), Config::default())?;
// Writes go through a short-lived writer lease; commit makes them durable + visible.
let mut w = index.writer()?;
w.upsert(1, &[("front", "the quick brown fox")])?;
w.upsert(2, &[("front", "the quack brown ox")])?;
w.commit()?;
drop(w);
// Reads go through a reader lease. A typo'd query still matches.
let hits = index.reader()?.matches("quikc brown", &SearchOpts::new(), 10)?;
assert!(hits.iter().any(|m| m.key.as_i64() == Some(1)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-data-model)The data model

A [ Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.Schema.html) declares a

**key**(its shape —

`Integer`/`Text`/`Blob`) plus named **text fields**. A

[is a](https://docs.rs/struct.Document.html)

`Document`[and a set of named segments (](https://docs.rs/enum.Key.html)

`Key``label → text`); a match
comes back as a [carrying the document key, the matched segment’s label, the matched byte span, and the segment’s text. There is no](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html)

`Match``doc` table: the key lives directly on each
segment row.[§](https://docs.rs#the-read-surface)The read surface

[ Reader::matches](https://docs.rs/struct.Reader.html#method.matches) is the eager default: the top

`limit` hydrated matches.
[is the lazy spine: a best-first](https://docs.rs/struct.Reader.html#method.candidates)

`Reader::candidates`[of provenance-only](https://docs.rs/struct.CandidateStream.html)

`CandidateStream`[s that a caller composes reranking, pagination, or fusion over, hydrating only what it keeps. Filtering is the opt-in](https://docs.rs/struct.Candidate.html)

`Candidate`[over the caller’s live data.](https://docs.rs/struct.SqlFilter.html)

`SqlFilter`[§](https://docs.rs#ingest-and-maintenance)Ingest and maintenance

Writes are cheap (a small delta append) and visible after [ commit](https://docs.rs/struct.Writer.html#method.commit).

[folds pending deltas;](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html#method.compact)

`compact`[is the signal that a compaction is due.](https://docs.rs/struct.Stats.html#structfield.delta_backlog)

`Stats::delta_backlog`[fully reindexes via an atomic shadow swap, which a tokenizer,](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html#method.rebuild)

`rebuild``data_version`, or schema change requires (each drops the cache on open).## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)

# sandpit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandpit/0.5.3/sandpit/

## Expand description

A concurrent, generational, trace and sweep garbage collected arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-an-arena)Creating An Arena

All garbage collection in Sandpit happens within an arena. Therefore, to be begin we can start with creating a new arena.

This can be done like so..

```
use sandpit::{Arena, Root};
// This creates an arena with a `MyRoot` as the root.
let gc: Arena<Root![MyRoot]> = Arena::new(|mutator| {
    MyRoot::new(mutator)
});
```
There are two big things to unpack here:

- An `Arena`is generic on its single Root value which it holds.
- The Root of an `Arena`must be a Higher Kinded Type(HKT).

This is explained in much further depth in [ sandpit::Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#trace-trait)Trace Trait

For a type to be GC’ed it is required to impl [ Trace](https://docs.rs/trait.Trace.html)
which can be safely derived as long as all inner types also impl

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Trace.html)

`Trace````
use sandpit::{Trace, Gc, GcOpt};
#[derive(Trace)]
enum Value<'gc> {
    // GC values must be branded with a mutation lifetime
    // to ensure freeing memory can happen safely.
    A(Gc<'gc, A>), // Mutable pointer to a garbage collected value
    B(GcOpt<'gc, B>), // Optionally null pointer that is also mutable. Can be unwrapped into a Gc.
}
// All inner values must be trace, therefore types A and B must impl Trace as well.
```
Essentially when a value is traced the tracer will mark the value as live, and call trace on all its inner pointers to GC values.

There are 2 types of GC pointers:

A type may also derive [ TraceLeaf](https://docs.rs/trait.TraceLeaf.html), if it contains no GC pointers.

[allows for easier interior mutability.](https://docs.rs/trait.TraceLeaf.html)

`TraceLeaf`[§](https://docs.rs#mutating-the-arena)Mutating the Arena

Once you have your arena and your traceable types, you can begin allocating
them in the arena by calling [ Arena::mutate](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.mutate). Within a mutation
we can essentially do 3 important things:

- Access all data reaachable from the root.
- Create new garbage collected values.
- Update Gc pointers to point to new values via a `WriteBarrier`

```
use sandpit::{Trace, Gc};
arena.mutate(|mutator, root| {
    // We can access everything reachable from the root.
    traverse(root);
    // We can allocate new Gc values.
    // Here is a pointer, to a pointer, to a bool!
    let gc_mut = Gc::new(mutator,
        Gc::new(mutator, true)
    );
    // We can mutate existing inner Gc and GcOpt pointers.
    gc_mut.write_barrier(mutator, |barrier| {
        barrier.set(Gc::new(mutator, false));
    })
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#collection-and-yielding)Collection and Yielding

In order for the Gc to free memory, and do so safely, all mutations must exit. Therefore, if a mutation involves a continuous loop of instructions, it must exit it’s mutation every so often to allow the GC to free memory.

The mutator exposes a signal([ Mutator::gc_yield](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutator.html#method.gc_yield)) which indicates if it is ready to free memory,
and that the mutation should end.

```
arena.mutate(|mutator, root| loop {
    // during this function it is likely the the GC will concurrently begin tracing!
    allocate_stuff(mutator, root);
    if mutator.gc_yield() {
        // the mutator is signaling to us that memory is ready to be freed so we should leave the mutation context
        break;
    } else {
        // if the mutator isn't signaling for us to yield then we
        // are fine to go on allocating more garbage
    }
});
```
* WARNING:* If a mutation continously runs without occasionally checking
the yield signal, memory cannot be freed!

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Root](https://docs.rs/macro.Root.html)
- Re-exported from ForLt. Used in making the root of an arena.
Produce `impl`types[ForLt](https://docs.rs/trait.Root.html)*on demand*.
- [field](https://docs.rs/macro.field.html)
- Exists to allow getting a write barrier to an inner field.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html)
- A concurrently garbage collected arena with a single root type.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.Config.html)
- This structure contains the configuration settings for a garbage collector.
- [Gc](https://docs.rs/struct.Gc.html)
- Immutable Gc pointer, meaning a write barrier cannot be used to update this pointer.
- [GcOpt](https://docs.rs/struct.GcOpt.html)
- A GC pointer which is able of pointing to null.
- [GcVec](https://docs.rs/struct.GcVec.html)
- [Inner](https://docs.rs/struct.InnerBarrier.html)- Barrier
- [Metrics](https://docs.rs/struct.Metrics.html)
- A ‘snapshot’ of the metrics relevant to the GC’s internal triggers.
- [Mutator](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutator.html)
- Allows for allocation and mutation within the GC arena.
- [Tagged](https://docs.rs/struct.Tagged.html)

- Allows for the mutation of `Gc``GcOpt`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [GcSync](https://docs.rs/trait.GcSync.html)
- [Root](https://docs.rs/trait.Root.html)
- Re-exported from ForLt. Used in making the root of an arena.
The main trait of the crate. The one expressing `: <'_>`-genericity.

# trifle_overlap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/trifle-overlap/0.5.0/trifle_overlap/

## Expand description

`trifle-overlap` — the weighted bit-sliced overlap engine, on the CRoaring backend.

Takes a set of postings (one bitmap per selected query token) with explicit non-negative
integer weights, and streams candidate ids in weighted-overlap (energy) order — highest
weighted score first. It knows nothing of SQL, segments, keys, text, provenance, or weighting
models — its surface is `(postings, weights) → impl Iterator<Item = Scored>`; the consumer
owns the weighting model (trifle feeds `Δ`-quantized logit-idf energies).

[§](https://docs.rs#energy-only-the-consumer-owns-the-raw-overlap-gate)Energy-only: the consumer owns the raw-overlap gate

The engine builds and walks the weighted bit-sliced counter only; it retains no copy of
the postings and reports no raw overlap. The consumer — which already holds the postings
and typically needs a per-id pass of its own (trifle fuses raw overlap with its count credit
in one `contains` sweep) — applies the raw-overlap floor to the yielded ids. What remains of
`min_shared` inside the engine is the scan bound ([ Counter::floor](https://docs.rs/struct.Counter.html#method.floor)): when every weight is

`≥ 1`, `weighted ≥ raw`, so score buckets
below the floor can only hold sub-floor candidates and are never scanned.[§](https://docs.rs#weight-0)Weight 0

Weights may be 0 (a common gram whose quantized energy is nothing). Such a gram adds no
energy to the planes, so a candidate matching *only* weight-0 grams has weighted score 0 and
is never surfaced by the walk — recovering those *count-only* candidates is the consumer’s
job. A weight-0 gram also breaks `weighted ≥ raw`, so the walk’s scan bound drops to 1 (every
positive bucket is scanned); the consumer’s raw-overlap gate stays sound either way.

[§](https://docs.rs#flatness)Flatness

Building the counter is `O(k·log k)` bitmap *operations* for `k` postings (the op count is
cardinality-independent); wall-clock is sublinear in cardinality (sparse) and flat in the
dense bitmap-container regime. More precisely, the build is `O(Σw·bits(Σw))` bitmap ops and
the walk visits at most `Σw` buckets of `bits(Σw)` plane ops each — so the honest bound is
parameterized by the weight sum, and the `O(k·log k)` reading holds because the consumer
bounds each weight by a constant ceiling (trifle: `⌊E_max/Δ⌉`, a `~log log N` quantity). See
*Weight preconditions* on [ Counter::build_weighted](https://docs.rs/struct.Counter.html#method.build_weighted).

```
use trifle_overlap::{Counter, Scored};
use croaring::Bitmap;
let a = Bitmap::of(&[1, 2, 3]);
let b = Bitmap::of(&[2, 3]);
let c = Bitmap::of(&[3]);
let counter = Counter::build_weighted(&[a, b, c], vec![1, 1, 1], 1);
let top: Vec<Scored> = counter.stream().collect();
assert_eq!(top[0].id, 3);      // in all three postings
assert_eq!(top[0].score, 3);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Counter](https://docs.rs/struct.Counter.html)
- The weighted bit-sliced overlap counter over a set of postings (CRoaring backend).
- [Counter](https://docs.rs/struct.CounterIter.html)- Iter
- The owning iterator returned by `Counter::stream`
- [Scored](https://docs.rs/struct.Scored.html)
- One scored candidate. `id`is an opaque posting id (a segment id, to trifle).`Copy`, 8 bytes, no allocation, no provenance. Raw overlap is not reported — the consumer, which holds the postings, computes it where needed (see the module docs).
- [Walk](https://docs.rs/struct.Walk.html)
- A plain, owned, `'static`walk cursor. The consumer owns both the`Counter``Walk`; neither borrows the other. Constructed via`Counter::walk`

# meerkat_mob - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/meerkat-mob/0.7.12/meerkat_mob/

## Expand description

Meerkat Mob - Multi-agent orchestration runtime.

This crate provides the runtime for orchestrating multiple agents as a collaborative mob. It handles member spawning, wiring, lifecycle management, and shared task coordination.

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

`meerkat-mob` is a plugin crate with a one-way dependency on the Meerkat
platform. No core Meerkat crate depends on this crate.

Key types:

- `MobDefinition`
- `MobEvent`- `MobEventKind`
- `MobEventStore`
- `MobStorage`

# cosmic-text 0.19.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cosmic-text/0.19.0

# COSMIC Text

Pure Rust multi-line text handling.

COSMIC Text provides advanced text shaping, layout, and rendering wrapped up into a simple abstraction. Shaping is provided by HarfRust, and supports a wide variety of advanced shaping operations. Rendering is provided by swash, which supports ligatures and color emoji. Layout is implemented custom, in safe Rust, and supports bidirectional text. Font fallback is also a custom implementation, reusing some of the static fallback lists in browsers such as Chromium and Firefox. Linux, macOS, and Windows are supported with the full feature set. Other platforms may need to implement font fallback capabilities.

## Screenshots

Arabic translation of Universal Declaration of Human Rights

Hindi translation of Universal Declaration of Human Rights

Simplified Chinese translation of Universal Declaration of Human Rights

## Roadmap

The following features must be supported before this is "ready":

-  Font loading (using fontdb)
- Preset fonts
- System fonts

-  Text styles (bold, italic, etc.)
- Per-buffer
- Per-span

-  Font shaping (using HarfRust)
- Cache results
- RTL
- Bidirectional rendering

-  Font fallback
- Choose font based on locale to work around "unification"
- Per-line granularity
- Per-character granularity

-  Font layout
- Click detection
- Simple wrapping
- Wrapping with indentation
- No wrapping
- Ellipsize

-  Font rendering (using swash)
- Cache results
- Font hinting
- Ligatures
- Color emoji

-  Text editing
- Performance improvements
- Text selection
-  Can automatically recreate [https://unicode.org/udhr/](https://unicode.org/udhr/)without errors (see below)
- Bidirectional selection
- Copy/paste

-  no_std support (with `default-features = false`)- no_std font loading
- no_std shaping
- no_std layout
- no_std rendering

The UDHR (Universal Declaration of Human Rights) test involves taking the entire
set of UDHR translations (almost 500 languages), concatenating them as one file
(which ends up being 8 megabytes!), then via the `editor-test` example,
automatically simulating the entry of that file into cosmic-text per-character,
with the use of backspace and delete tested per character and per line. Then,
the final contents of the buffer is compared to the original file. All of the
106746 lines are correct.

# cosmic_text - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cosmic-text/0.19.0/cosmic_text/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cosmic-text)COSMIC Text

This library provides advanced text handling in a generic way. It provides abstractions for shaping, font discovery, font fallback, layout, rasterization, and editing. Shaping utilizes harfrust, font discovery utilizes fontdb, and the rasterization is optional and utilizes swash. The other features are developed internal to this library.

It is recommended that you start by creating a [ FontSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.FontSystem.html), after which you can create a

[, provide it with some text, and then inspect the layout it produces. At this point, you can use the](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)

`Buffer``SwashCache` to rasterize glyphs into either images or pixels.```
use cosmic_text::{Attrs, Color, FontSystem, SwashCache, Buffer, Metrics, Shaping};
// A FontSystem provides access to detected system fonts, create one per application
let mut font_system = FontSystem::new();
// A SwashCache stores rasterized glyphs, create one per application
let mut swash_cache = SwashCache::new();
// Text metrics indicate the font size and line height of a buffer
let metrics = Metrics::new(14.0, 20.0);
// A Buffer provides shaping and layout for a UTF-8 string, create one per text widget
let mut buffer = Buffer::new(&mut font_system, metrics);
// Borrow buffer together with the font system for more convenient method calls
let mut buffer = buffer.borrow_with(&mut font_system);
// Attributes indicate what font to choose
let attrs = Attrs::new();
// Set size and text
buffer.set_size(Some(80.0), Some(25.0));
buffer.set_text("Hello, Rust! 🦀\n", &attrs, Shaping::Advanced, None);
// Inspect the output runs
for run in buffer.layout_runs() {
    for glyph in run.glyphs.iter() {
        println!("{:#?}", glyph);
    }
}
// Create a default text color
let text_color = Color::rgb(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF);
// Draw the buffer (for performance, instead use SwashCache directly)
buffer.draw(&mut swash_cache, text_color, |x, y, w, h, color| {
    // Fill in your code here for drawing rectangles
});
```

# cosmic_text/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT OR Apache-2.0
[2](https://docs.rs#2)
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! # COSMIC Text
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! This library provides advanced text handling in a generic way. It provides abstractions for
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! shaping, font discovery, font fallback, layout, rasterization, and editing. Shaping utilizes
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! harfrust, font discovery utilizes fontdb, and the rasterization is optional and utilizes
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! swash. The other features are developed internal to this library.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! It is recommended that you start by creating a [`FontSystem`], after which you can create a
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! [`Buffer`], provide it with some text, and then inspect the layout it produces. At this
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! point, you can use the `SwashCache` to rasterize glyphs into either images or pixels.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! ```
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! use cosmic_text::{Attrs, Color, FontSystem, SwashCache, Buffer, Metrics, Shaping};
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! // A FontSystem provides access to detected system fonts, create one per application
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! let mut font_system = FontSystem::new();
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! // A SwashCache stores rasterized glyphs, create one per application
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! let mut swash_cache = SwashCache::new();
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! // Text metrics indicate the font size and line height of a buffer
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! let metrics = Metrics::new(14.0, 20.0);
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! // A Buffer provides shaping and layout for a UTF-8 string, create one per text widget
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! let mut buffer = Buffer::new(&mut font_system, metrics);
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! // Borrow buffer together with the font system for more convenient method calls
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! let mut buffer = buffer.borrow_with(&mut font_system);
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! // Attributes indicate what font to choose
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! let attrs = Attrs::new();
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! // Set size and text
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! buffer.set_size(Some(80.0), Some(25.0));
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! buffer.set_text("Hello, Rust! 🦀\n", &attrs, Shaping::Advanced, None);
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! // Inspect the output runs
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! for run in buffer.layout_runs() {
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!     for glyph in run.glyphs.iter() {
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!         println!("{:#?}", glyph);
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!     }
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! }
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! // Create a default text color
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! let text_color = Color::rgb(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF);
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! // Draw the buffer (for performance, instead use SwashCache directly)
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! buffer.draw(&mut swash_cache, text_color, |x, y, w, h, color| {
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!     // Fill in your code here for drawing rectangles
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! });
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! ```

[146](https://docs.rs#146)type HashMap<K, V> = std::collections::HashMap<K, V, BuildHasher>;
[147](https://docs.rs#147)#[cfg(not(feature = "std"))]
[148](https://docs.rs#148)type HashMap<K, V> = hashbrown::HashMap<K, V, BuildHasher>;

### impl [FontSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.FontSystem.html)

Create a new [ FontSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.FontSystem.html), that allows access to any installed system fonts

[§](https://docs.rs#timing)Timing

This function takes some time to run. On the release build, it can take up to a second,
while debug builds can take up to ten times longer. For this reason, it should only be
called once, and the resulting [ FontSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.FontSystem.html) should be shared.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/buffer.rs.html#66-113)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/buffer.rs.html#66-113)

Return an iterator of `(x_left, x_width)` pixel spans for the highlighted areas
between `cursor_start` and `cursor_end` within this run.

For pure LTR or pure RTL runs this yields at most one span. For mixed BiDi runs (where selected and unselected glyphs interleave visually) it yields multiple disjoint spans.

Returns an empty iterator if the cursor range does not intersect this run.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/buffer.rs.html#120-142)#### pub fn [cursor_position](https://docs.rs#method.cursor_position)(&self, cursor: &[Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/buffer.rs.html#120-142)

#### pub fn [cursor_position](https://docs.rs#method.cursor_position)(&self, cursor: &[Cursor](https://docs.rs/struct.Cursor.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html)>

Returns the visual x position (in pixels) of `cursor` within this run,
or `None` if the cursor does not belong to this run.

For RTL glyphs the cursor is placed at the right edge minus the offset; for LTR glyphs it is placed at the left edge plus the offset.

Find which glyph in this run contains `cursor`, returning
`(glyph_index, pixel_offset_within_glyph)`, or `None` if the cursor
is not on this run.

`PartialOrd`[with those of another. The comparison works like short-circuit evaluation, returning a result without comparing the remaining elements. As soon as an order can be determined, the evaluation stops and a result is returned.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/iterator/trait.Iterator.html)

# LineEnding in cosmic_text - Rust

```
pub enum LineEnding {
    Lf,
    CrLf,
    Cr,
    LfCr,
    None,
}
```
## Expand description

Line ending

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Lf)

### Lf

Use `\n` for line ending (POSIX-style)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CrLf)

### CrLf

Use `\r\n` for line ending (Windows-style)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Cr)

### Cr

Use `\r` for line ending (many legacy systems)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LfCr)

### LfCr

Use `\n\r` for line ending (some legacy systems)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.None)

### None

No line ending

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/edit/vi.rs.html#269-272)#### pub fn [save_point](https://docs.rs#method.save_point)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cosmic_text/edit/vi.rs.html#269-272)

#### pub fn [save_point](https://docs.rs#method.save_point)(&mut self)

Set current change as the save (or pivot) point.

A pivot point is the last saved index. Anything before or after the pivot indicates that the editor has been changed or is unsaved.

Undoing changes down to the pivot point sets the editor as unchanged. Redoing changes up to the pivot point sets the editor as unchanged.

Undoing or redoing changes beyond the pivot point sets the editor to changed.

## Expand description

Helper for caching a value when the value is optionally present in the ‘unused’ state.

Gets the value if in state `Self::Used`.

Gets the value mutably if in state `Self::Used`.

Checks if the value is empty or unused.

Checks if the value is used (i.e. cached for access).

Checks if the value was previously cached but has been invalidated.

Takes the buffered value if in state `Self::Unused`.

Takes the cached value if in state `Self::Used`.

Moves the value from `Self::Used` to `Self::Unused`.

Sets the value to `Self::Used`.

# Command in cosmic_text - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cosmic-text/0.19.0/cosmic_text/enum.Command.html

```
pub enum Command {
    MoveTo(
```
[Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html)),
    LineTo([Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html)),
    CurveTo([Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html), [Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html), [Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html)),
    QuadTo([Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html), [Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html)),
    Close,
}## Expand description

Path command.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.MoveTo)

### MoveTo([Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html))

Begins a new subpath at the specified point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LineTo)

### LineTo([Vector](https://docs.rs/zeno/0.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/zeno/geometry/struct.Vector.html))

A straight line from the previous point to the specified point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CurveTo)

A cubic bezier curve from the previous point to the final point with two intermediate control points.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.QuadTo)

A quadratic curve from the previous point to the final point with one intermediate control point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Close)

### Close

Closes a subpath, connecting the final point to the initial point.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# EllipsizeHeightLimit in cosmic_text - Rust

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Lines)

### Lines([usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html))

Number of lines to show before ellipsizing the rest. Only works if `Wrap` is NOT set to
`Wrap::None`. Otherwise, it will be ignored and the behavior will be the same as `Lines(1)`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Height)

### Height([f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html))

Ellipsizes the last line that fits within the given height limit. If `Wrap` is set to
`Wrap::None`, the behavior will be the same as `Lines(1)`

# Family in cosmic_text - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cosmic-text/0.19.0/cosmic_text/enum.Family.html

```
pub enum Family<'a> {
    Name(&'a
```
[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)),
    Serif,
    SansSerif,
    Cursive,
    Fantasy,
    Monospace,
}## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Name)

### Name(&'a [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html))

The name of a font family of choice.

This must be a *Typographic Family* (ID 16) or a *Family Name* (ID 1) in terms of TrueType.
Meaning you have to pass a family without any additional suffixes like *Bold*, *Italic*,
*Regular*, etc.

Localized names are allowed.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Serif)

### Serif

Serif fonts represent the formal text style for a script.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SansSerif)

### SansSerif

Glyphs in sans-serif fonts, as the term is used in CSS, are generally low contrast and have stroke endings that are plain — without any flaring, cross stroke, or other ornamentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Cursive)

### Cursive

Glyphs in cursive fonts generally use a more informal script style, and the result looks more like handwritten pen or brush writing than printed letterwork.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Fantasy)

### Fantasy

Fantasy fonts are primarily decorative or expressive fonts that contain decorative or expressive representations of characters.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Monospace)

### Monospace

The sole criterion of a monospace font is that all glyphs have the same fixed width.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

# Shaping in cosmic_text - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cosmic-text/0.19.0/cosmic_text/enum.Shaping.html

```
pub enum Shaping {
    Basic,
    Advanced,
}
```
## Expand description

The shaping strategy of some text.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Basic)

### Basic

Basic shaping with no font fallback.

This shaping strategy is very cheap, but it will not display complex scripts properly nor try to find missing glyphs in your system fonts.

You should use this strategy when you have complete control of the text and the font you are displaying in your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Advanced)

### Advanced

Advanced text shaping and font fallback.

You will need to enable this strategy if the text contains a complex script, the font used needs it, and/or multiple fonts in your system may be needed to display all of the glyphs.

# Fallback in cosmic_text - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cosmic-text/0.19.0/cosmic_text/trait.Fallback.html

`pub trait Fallback: `[Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) {
    // Required methods
    fn [common_fallback](https://docs.rs#tymethod.common_fallback)(&self) -> &[&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)];
[forbidden_fallback](https://docs.rs#tymethod.forbidden_fallback)(&self) -> &[&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)];
[script_fallback](https://docs.rs#tymethod.script_fallback)(&self, script: [Script](https://docs.rs/unicode-script/0.5.8/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/unicode_script/tables/tables_impl/enum.Script.html), locale: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> &[&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)];
}## Expand description

The `Fallback` trait allows for configurable font fallback lists to be set during construction of the [ FontSystem](https://docs.rs/struct.FontSystem.html).

A custom fallback list can be added via the [ FontSystem::new_with_locale_and_db_and_fallback](https://docs.rs/struct.FontSystem.html#method.new_with_locale_and_db_and_fallback) constructor.

A default implementation is provided by the [ PlatformFallback](https://docs.rs/struct.PlatformFallback.html) struct, which encapsulates the target platform’s pre-configured fallback lists.

```
struct MyFallback;
impl Fallback for MyFallback {
    fn common_fallback(&self) -> &[&'static str] {
        &[
            "Segoe UI",
            "Segoe UI Emoji",
            "Segoe UI Symbol",
            "Segoe UI Historic",
        ]
    }
    fn forbidden_fallback(&self) -> &[&'static str] {
        &[]
    }
    fn script_fallback(&self, script: Script, locale: &str) -> &[&'static str] {
        match script {
            Script::Adlam => &["Ebrima"],
            Script::Bengali => &["Nirmala UI"],
            Script::Canadian_Aboriginal => &["Gadugi"],
            // ...
            _ => &[],
       }
    }
}
let locale = "en-US".to_string();
let db = fontdb::Database::new();
let font_system = FontSystem::new_with_locale_and_db_and_fallback(locale, db, MyFallback);
```

---

# render_decoration in cosmic_text - Rust

`pub fn render_decoration<R: `[Renderer](https://docs.rs/trait.Renderer.html)>(
    renderer: [&mut R](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
    run: &[LayoutRun](https://docs.rs/struct.LayoutRun.html)<'_>,
    default_color: [Color](https://docs.rs/struct.Color.html),
)## Expand description

Draw text decoration lines (underline, strikethrough, overline) for a layout run.

# bitflags 2.13.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bitflags/^2.10.0

# bitflags

`bitflags` generates flags enums with well-defined semantics and ergonomic end-user APIs.

You can use `bitflags` to:

- provide more user-friendly bindings to C APIs where flags may or may not be fully known in advance.
- generate efficient options types with string parsing and formatting support.

You can't use `bitflags` to:

-
guarantee only bits corresponding to defined flags will ever be set. `bitflags`allows access to the underlying bits type so arbitrary bits may be set.
-
define bitfields. `bitflags`only generates types where set bits denote the presence of some combination of flags.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "2.13.0"
```
and this to your source code:

```
use bitflags;
```
## Example

Generate a flags structure:

```
use bitflags;
// The `bitflags!` macro generates `struct`s that manage a set of flags.
bitflags!
```
## Cargo features

The `bitflags` library defines a few Cargo features that you can opt-in to:

- `std`: Implement the- `Error`trait on error types used by- `bitflags`.
- `serde`: Support deriving- `serde`traits on generated flags types.
- `arbitrary`: Support deriving- `arbitrary`traits on generated flags types.
- `bytemuck`: Support deriving- `bytemuck`traits on generated flags types.

Also see [ bitflags_derive](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags-derive) for other flags-aware traits.

## Rust Version Support

The minimum supported Rust version is documented in the `Cargo.toml` file.
This may be bumped in minor releases as necessary.

# cosmic_undo_2 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cosmic_undo_2/^0.2.0

# Undo done the right way!

## Introduction

An undo crate that makes it so that, the instant you edit something you undid
to, instead of truncating the undo/redo history, it bakes the rewind onto the
end of the Undo history as a precursor to your new change. The idea originates
from (and all the credits goes to) [zaboople/klonk](https://github.com/zaboople/klonk/blob/master/TheGURQ.md). This crate is an
implementation of this idea with a minor variation explained below.

As an example consider the following sequence of commands:

| Command | State |
|---|---|
| Init | |
| Do A | A |
| Do B | A, B |
| Undo | A |
| Do C | A, C |

With the **classical undo**, repeated undo would lead to the sequence:

| Command | State |
|---|---|
| A, C | |
| Undo | A |
| Undo |

Starting from 5, with **undo_2**, repeating undo would lead to the sequence:

| Command | State |
|---|---|
| A, C | |
| Undo | A |
| Undo | A,B |
| Undo | A |
| Undo |

**undo_2**'s undo navigates back in history, while classical undo navigates back
through the sequence of command that builds the state.

## Features

- historical undo sequence, no commands are lost.
- user-friendly compared to complex undo trees.
- optimized implementation: no commands are ever copied.
- very lightweight, dumb and simple.
- possibility to merge and splice commands.

## How to use it

Add the dependency to the cargo file:

```
[dependencies]
undo_2 = "0.1"
```
Then add this to your source file:

```
use undo_2::Commands;
```
The example below implements a dumb text editor. *undo_2* does not perform
itself "undos" and "redos", rather, it returns a sequence of commands that must
be interpreted by the application. This design pattern makes implementation
easier because it is not necessary to borrow data within the stored list of
commands.

```
use undo_2::{Commands,Action};
enum Command {
    Add(char),
    Delete(char),
}
struct TextEditor {
    text: String,
    command: Commands<Command>,
}
impl TextEditor {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            text: String::new(),
            command: Commands::new(),
        }
    }
    pub fn add_char(&mut self, c: char) {
        self.text.push(c);
        self.command.push(Command::Add(c));
    }
    pub fn delete_char(&mut self) {
        if let Some(c) = self.text.pop() {
            self.command.push(Command::Delete(c));
        }
    }
    pub fn undo(&mut self) {
        for action in self.command.undo() {
            interpret_action(&mut self.text, action)
        }
    }
    pub fn redo(&mut self) {
        for action in self.command.redo() {
            interpret_action(&mut self.text, action)
        }
    }
}
fn interpret_action(data: &mut String, action: Action<&Command>) {
    use Command::*;
    match action {
        Action::Do(Add(c)) | Action::Undo(Delete(c)) => {
            data.push(*c);
        }
        Action::Undo(Add(_)) | Action::Do(Delete(_)) => {
            data.pop();
        }
    }
}
let mut editor = TextEditor::new();
editor.add_char('a'); //              :[1]
editor.add_char('b'); //              :[2]
editor.add_char('d'); //              :[3]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abd");
editor.undo(); // first undo          :[4]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.add_char('c'); //              :[5]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abc");
editor.undo(); // Undo [5]            :[6]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.undo(); // Undo the undo [4]   :[7]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abd");
editor.undo(); // Undo [3]            :[8]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.undo(); // Undo [2]            :[9]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "a");
```
## More information

- After a sequence of consecutive undo, if a new command is added, the undos forming the sequence are merged. This makes the traversal of the undo sequence more concise by avoiding state duplication.

| Command | State | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Init | ||
| Do A | A | |
| Do B | A,B | |
| Do C | A, B, C | |
| Undo | A, B | Merged |
| Undo | A | Merged |
| Do D | A, D | |
| Undo | A | Redo the 2 Merged Undo |
| Undo | A, B, C | |
| Undo | A, B | |
| Undo | A | |
| Undo |

- Each execution of an undos or redo may lead to the execution of a sequence of
actions in the form `Undo(a)+Do(b)+Do(c)`. Basic arithmetic is implemented assuming that`Do(a)+Undo(a)`is equivalent to not doing anything (here the 2`a`'s designate the same entity, not to equal objects).

The piece of code below, which is the longer version of the code above, illustrates points 1 and 2.

```
let mut editor = TextEditor::new();
editor.add_char('a'); //              :[1]
editor.add_char('b'); //              :[2]
editor.add_char('d'); //              :[3]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abd");
editor.undo(); // first undo          :[4]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.add_char('c'); //              :[5]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abc");
editor.undo(); // Undo [5]            :[6]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.undo(); // Undo the undo [4]   :[7]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abd");
editor.undo(); // Undo [3]            :[8]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.undo(); // Undo [2]            :[9]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "a");
editor.add_char('z'); //              :[10]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "az");
// when an action is performed after a sequence
// of undo, the undos are merged: undos [6] to [9] are merged now
editor.undo(); // back to [10]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "a");
editor.undo(); // back to [5]: reverses the consecutive sequence of undos in batch
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abc");
editor.undo(); // back to [4]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.undo(); // back to [3]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abd");
editor.undo(); // back to [2]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.undo(); // back to [1]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "a");
editor.undo(); // back to [0]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "");
editor.redo(); // back to [1]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "a");
editor.redo(); // back to [2]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.redo(); // back to [3]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abd");
editor.redo(); // back to [4]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "ab");
editor.redo(); // back to [5]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "abc");
editor.redo(); // back to [9]: redo inner consecutive sequence of undos in batch
               //              (undo are merged only when they are not the last action)
assert_eq!(editor.text, "a");
editor.redo(); // back to [10]
assert_eq!(editor.text, "az");
editor.add_char('1');
editor.add_char('2');
assert_eq!(editor.text, "az12");
editor.undo();
editor.undo();
assert_eq!(editor.text, "az");
editor.redo(); // undo is the last action, undo the undo only once
assert_eq!(editor.text, "az1");
editor.redo();
assert_eq!(editor.text, "az12");
```
## Crate features

`serde`: enabled by default

# fontdb 0.23.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fontdb/^0.23

# fontdb

`fontdb` is a simple, in-memory font database with CSS-like queries.

## Features

- The database can load fonts from files, directories and raw data (`Vec<u8>`).
- The database can match a font using CSS-like queries. See `Database::query`.
- The database can try to load system fonts. Currently, this is implemented by scanning predefined directories. The library does not interact with the system API.
- Provides a unique ID for each font face.

## Non-goals

-
Advanced font properties querying. The database provides only storage and matching capabilities. For font properties querying you can use [ttf-parser](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/ttf-parser).
-
A font fallback mechanism. This library can be used to implement a font fallback mechanism, but it doesn't implement one.
-
Application's global database. The database doesn't use `static`, therefore it's up to the caller where it should be stored.
-
Font types support other than TrueType.

## Font vs Face

A font is a collection of font faces. Therefore, a font face is a subset of a font. A simple font (*.ttf/*.otf) usually contains a single font face, but a font collection (*.ttc) can contain multiple font faces.

`fontdb` stores and matches font faces, not fonts.
Therefore, after loading a font collection with 5 faces (for example), the database will be
populated with 5 `FaceInfo` objects, all of which will be pointing to the same file or binary data.

## Performance

The database performance is largely limited by the storage itself.
We are using [ttf-parser](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/ttf-parser), so the parsing should not be a bottleneck.

For example, on Mac Book Pro 14 with M1 Pro, it takes just ~24ms to load 1361 font faces.

## Safety

The library relies on memory-mapped files, which is inherently unsafe. But since we do not keep the files open it should be perfectly safe.

If you would like to use a persistent memory mapping of the font files,
then you can use the unsafe `Database::make_shared_face_data` function.

## License

MIT

# hashbrown 0.17.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hashbrown/^0.17

# hashbrown

This crate is a Rust port of Google's high-performance [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) hash map,
adapted to make it a drop-in replacement for Rust's standard `HashMap` and
`HashSet` types.

The original C++ version of SwissTable can be found [here](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/master/absl/container/internal/raw_hash_set.h), and this
[CppCon talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncHmEUmJZf4) gives an overview of how the algorithm works.

Since Rust 1.36, the Rust standard library has adopted this implementation for
`HashMap`, using its own default hasher (see
[ std::hash::DefaultHasher](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/hash/struct.DefaultHasher.html)).
However you may still want to use this crate instead since it works in
environments without

`std`, such as embedded systems and kernels.## Features

- Drop-in replacement for the standard library `HashMap`and`HashSet`types.
- Uses [foldhash](https://github.com/orlp/foldhash)as the default hasher, which is much faster than SipHash. However, foldhash does*not provide the same level of HashDoS resistance*as SipHash, so if that is important to you, you might want to consider using a different hasher.
- Around 2x faster than the previous standard library `HashMap`.
- Lower memory usage: only 1 byte of overhead per entry instead of 8.
- Compatible with `#[no_std]`(but requires a global allocator with the`alloc`crate).
- Empty hash maps do not allocate any memory.
- SIMD lookups to scan multiple hash entries in parallel.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.17"
```
Then:

```
use HashMap;
let mut map = new;
map.insert;
```
## Flags

This crate has the following Cargo features:

- `nightly`: Enables nightly-only features including:- `#[may_dangle]`.
- `serde`: Enables serde serialization support.
- `rayon`: Enables rayon parallel iterator support.
- `equivalent`: Allows comparisons to be customized with the- `Equivalent`trait. (enabled by default)
- `raw-entry`: Enables access to the deprecated- `RawEntry`API.
- `inline-more`: Adds inline hints to most functions, improving run-time performance at the cost of compilation time. (enabled by default)
- `default-hasher`: Compiles with foldhash as default hasher. (enabled by default)
- `allocator-api2`: Enables support for allocators that support- `allocator-api2`. (enabled by default)

# log 0.4.33 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/log/^0.4.29

# log

A Rust library providing a lightweight logging *facade*.

A logging facade provides a single logging API that abstracts over the actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

## Minimum supported `rustc`

See the `rust-version` field in `Cargo.toml` for the current minimum Rust toolchain version.

This version is explicitly tested in CI and may be bumped in any release as needed. Maintaining compatibility with older compilers is a priority though, so the bar for bumping the minimum supported version is set very high. Any changes to the supported minimum version will be called out in the release notes.

## Usage

### In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided macros to
log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
```
use ;
```
### In executables

In order to produce log output, executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some options:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct [an FFI-safe wrapper over](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/421)to initialize in your libraries.`log`

- You may need to construct
- Utilities:

Executables should choose a logger implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logger implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the logger is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

## Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature, you can associate structured data with your log records:

```
use ;
```

# rustc-hash 2.1.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustc-hash/^2.1.1

# rustc-hash

A speedy, non-cryptographic hashing algorithm used by `rustc`.
The [hash map in  std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.HashMap.html) uses SipHash by default, which provides resistance against DOS attacks.
These attacks aren't a concern in the compiler so we prefer to use a quicker,
non-cryptographic hash algorithm.

The original hash algorithm provided by this crate was one taken from Firefox, hence the hasher it provides is called FxHasher. This name is kept for backwards compatibility, but the underlying hash has since been replaced. The current design for the hasher is a polynomial hash finished with a single bit rotation, together with a wyhash-inspired compression function for strings/slices, both designed by Orson Peters.

For `rustc` we have tried many different hashing algorithms. Hashing speed is
critical, especially for single integers. Spending more CPU cycles on a higher
quality hash does not reduce hash collisions enough to make the compiler faster
on real-world benchmarks.

## Usage

This crate provides `FxHashMap` and `FxHashSet` as collections.
They are simply type aliases for their `std::collection` counterparts using the Fx hasher.

```
use FxHashMap;
let mut map:  = default;
map.insert;
```
`no_std`

The `std` feature is on by default to enable collections.
It can be turned off in `Cargo.toml` like so:

```
 = {  = "2.1",  = false }
```

# smol_str 0.3.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/smol_str/^0.3.2

# smol_str

A `SmolStr` is a string type that has the following properties:

- `size_of::<SmolStr>() == 24`(therefore- `== size_of::<String>()`on 64 bit platforms)
- `Clone`is- `O(1)`
- Strings are stack-allocated if they are:
- Up to 23 bytes long
- Longer than 23 bytes, but substrings of `WS`(see`src/lib.rs`). Such strings consist solely of consecutive newlines, followed by consecutive spaces

- If a string does not satisfy the aforementioned conditions, it is heap-allocated
- Additionally, a `SmolStr`can be explicitly created from a`&'static str`without allocation

Unlike `String`, however, `SmolStr` is immutable. The primary use case for
`SmolStr` is a good enough default storage for tokens of typical programming
languages. Strings consisting of a series of newlines, followed by a series of
whitespace are a typical pattern in computer programs because of indentation.
Note that a specialized interner might be a better solution for some use cases.

## Benchmarks

```
```

# sys-locale

A small and lightweight Rust library to get the current active locale on the system.

`sys-locale` is small library to get the current locale set for the system or application with the relevant platform APIs. The library is also `no_std` compatible, relying only on `alloc`, except on Linux and BSD.

- macOS

- WebAssembly, for the following platforms:
- Inside of a web browser (via the `js`feature)
- Emscripten (via the `UNIX`backend) Further support for other WASM targets is dependent on upstream support in those target's runtimes and specifications.

- Inside of a web browser (via the
- Windows
